title: 2026 in Review: The Year Telecom Put AI to Work
summary: New article for Telcos by RADCOM: 2026 in Review: The Year Telecom Put AI to Work From agentic AI and Level 4 autonomous networks to 5G SA slicing and the first 6G standards, discover the telecom trends that defined 2026.
body_markdown:
If 2025 was the year agentic AI arrived, 2026 was the year operators put it into production. Across the industry, the conversation shifted from pilots and proofs of concept to AI agents running live networks, 5G standalone proving its value in slicing, FWA, and private networks, and the first concrete steps toward 6G. It was also a year of hard questions about cost, customer trust in AI, and return on investment.


As we head into 2027, here are the key themes that defined the past twelve months, and how they compare with the[operator priorities for 2026](https://radcom.com/operator-priorities-for-2026-and-beyond-data-automation-customer-experience/) we highlighted in January.


## The Untapped Promise of 5G


5G has been around for years, but 2026 showed how much of its potential is still untapped. According to the[Ericsson Mobility Report](https://www.ericsson.com/en/reports-and-papers/mobility-report) , 5G subscriptions are now close to 3.3 billion, and mobile network data traffic grew 23% between Q2 2025 and Q2 2026. Yet while more than 390 operators have launched commercial 5G, fewer than 100 have deployed 5G standalone (5G SA) cores, so many consumers still experience 5G as a faster 4G.


The bigger story, however, is how operators approached its monetization. With consumers rarely paying extra for a 5G icon, operators focused on three areas that are proving their value. Fixed wireless access (FWA) remains the biggest consumer success, with 71% of FWA providers now offering it over 5G. More than 1,000 organizations now run private 5G networks. And where 5G SA is live, slicing is becoming a product, with commercial offerings rising from[65 to 84 in just six months](https://www.ericsson.com/en/reports-and-papers/mobility-report) . However, turning slicing into a commercial offering requires operators to guarantee the performance of each slice. This is where RADCOM helps, providing real-time assurance that[slice SLAs](https://radcom.com/solutions/network-monitoring/) are being met.


5G itself also moved forward, with 19 operators launching commercial 5G-Advanced services, bringing greater intelligence, efficiency, and performance to their networks. Monetizing 5G remains a work in progress, but operators now have the foundations for new revenue models in place.


## AI Moves from Copilot to Agent


This was the year agentic AI went live. By April 2026,[IDC found](https://info.idc.com/state-of-the-telco-market.html) that the average telecom operator already had around 10 AI agents in production, with plans to double that by year end. The results are tangible: one operator increased its net promoter score (NPS) by 135%, while another recovered 300 hours of productivity a week. That said, AI agents are only as good as the data they act on. In our[January survey](https://www.gsmaintelligence.com/research/service-assurance-trends-in-the-ai-era) with GSMA Intelligence, 58% of operators rated real-time data as “extremely important” for automating network operations, which is why RADCOM launched[RADCOM ADM (Analytics Designer Module)](https://radcom.com/radcom-adm/) this year, letting operators create KPIs in real time, at resolutions as fine as 10 seconds, and feed trusted metrics to their AI agents.


AI also moved directly into the radio layer. In live trials, AI-managed beamforming boosted[downlink throughput by 16%](https://www.t-mobile.com/news/network/5g-advanced-in-action-better-experiences-t-mobile-puts-ai-to-work-for-customers) and spectral efficiency by 12%, while other AI-RAN trials verified[spectral efficiency gains of](https://www.telecomstechnews.com/news/nokia-ai-ran-trials-yield-spectral-efficiency-gain/) 20%. Meanwhile, AI-driven energy saving, which puts unused radios into deep sleep during low-traffic hours, has delivered[RAN energy savings of 15%](https://inform.tmforum.org/research-and-analysis/proofs-of-concept/how-to-reduce-ran-energy-usage-by-a-quarter-with-predictive-ai) in a TM Forum Catalyst, with savings of up to 25% expected.


## Autonomous Networks Reach Level 4


Autonomous networks moved from roadmap to reality. A growing number of operators have achieved[TM Forum validation](https://web.tmforum.org/welcome/an-journey-starts-here) for Level 4 autonomy in parts of their live networks. Asia-Pacific operators are leading the way, with North America, Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East close behind.


However, there is still a long way to go. The industry average sits at around Level 2 to Level 3, and roughly[81% of operators](https://www.tmforum.org/news-insight/newsroom/autonomous-networks-leadership-forum-spotlights-level-4-shift) are targeting broad Level 4 maturity across their core domains by 2030. The constraint is no longer the quality of AI models, but whether operators have the data, policy controls, and platforms that allow agents to act safely. At the beginning of the year, 38% of operators still lacked a unified data foundation, which is a gap[RADCOM ACE](https://radcom.com/products/radcom-ace/) is designed to close.


## 6G Takes Shape


While 5G matured, 6G began to take shape. In February,[ITU experts](https://www.itu.int/hub/2026/04/direct-to-device-services-poised-for-the-leap-to-6g/) agreed on the performance requirements for IMT-2030 (6G), with native AI integration and integrated sensing and communication among the six pillars. Meanwhile, 3GPP is finalizing Release 20, which completes 5G-Advanced and starts the 6G study work, ahead of the first 6G specifications in Release 21 (2028 to 2029). The first commercial 6G services are expected around 2030.


The message for operators is clear: the AI and automation capabilities built on 5G SA today are[the foundation for 6G tomorrow](https://radcom.com/the-case-for-assurance-in-6g/) .


## What Else Stood Out?


Beyond 5G, 6G, and AI, a few other trends deserve a mention:


- **The cost of AI.** AI is competing with telecom for the same semiconductor wafers,[driving up the price of chips](https://www.lightreading.com/5g/ai-is-making-telecom-more-expensive-warn-ericsson-and-nokia) used in network equipment, costs that are likely to filter through to consumer tariffs. Gartner also found that organizations are spending[18 times more](https://www.varindia.com/news/gartner-warns-ai-risks-are-outpacing-business-value) to achieve positive AI returns than they did two years ago. This is why[assurance modernization should be the first investment in autonomy](https://radcom.com/why-assurance-modernisation-should-be-the-first-investment-in-autonomy/) . It lowers operating costs today, with operators that moved to RADCOM[cutting assurance CAPEX and OPEX by around 40%](https://radcom.com/why-radcom/) , while creating the trusted intelligence AI needs to scale.
- **The trust gap.** Customers are not as comfortable with AI as operators might hope.[Only 47% of consumers](https://www.telecomstechnews.com/news/telcos-race-ahead-on-ai-managed-customer-experience-plans/) are comfortable with AI inferring information about them, even though 92% of telco leaders believe customers will grow comfortable with it. A[TELUS Digital poll](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/nearly-half-of-regular-u-s-ai-users-say-they-have-bent-the-truth-to-get-past-ai-customer-service-new-telus-digital-poll-finds-882074321.html) found that 77% of regular AI users said a guaranteed human support option would make them more likely to choose one company over another. Closing that gap[depends on governance](https://radcom.com/governing-ai-agents-in-telecom-networks/) : clear guardrails, accountability, and human oversight for every AI agent acting on the network.
- **Customer experience goes proactive.** In January, 52% of operators told us analyzing customer experience to reduce churn was a top data priority. In 2026,[NVIDIA’s State of AI in Telecommunications 2026 survey](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/lp/industries/telecommunications/state-of-ai-in-telecom-survey-report/) found that network automation overtook customer experience as the leading AI use case, but the two are converging, with leading operators using AI to[link network performance directly to customer satisfaction](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/technology-media-and-telecommunications/our-insights/telcos-ai-inflection-point-what-leaders-do-to-capture-value) and retention.
- **New revenue from AI traffic.** In an[Omdia survey](https://www.lightreading.com/ai-machine-learning/riding-the-ai-wave-an-omdia-survey-of-telecom-providers) , 61% of telecom providers identified high bandwidth wavelength services as one of their top two revenue opportunities from AI, as inference workloads spread across enterprises.


## Looking Ahead to 2027


2026 proved that AI can deliver real value in telecom. Several of the priorities operators identified in our[January survey](https://www.gsmaintelligence.com/research/service-assurance-trends-in-the-ai-era?utm_source=chatgpt.com) gained momentum, as agentic AI advanced toward production and automation took center stage. The industry is moving beyond AI experimentation, with a growing focus on putting intelligence to work across network operations.


Heading into 2027, the question is no longer whether to deploy AI, but how to scale it profitably, securely, and in ways that earn customer trust. Operators with clean, unified data, end-to-end visibility, and strong governance will be best positioned to turn AI ambition into measurable business impact.
